stories.title: OpenAI's frontier models and Codex are coming to Google Cloud
paragraphs: OpenAI announced on Oct. 21 that it is partnering with Google Cloud to bring its frontier models and its Codex agentic coding workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden. According to OpenAI, the integration will give Google Cloud customers native access to the models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud's data governance and infrastructure.

OpenAI says Google Cloud customers will be able to buy OpenAI frontier models through Model Garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace, and that enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw those commitments down for these purchases. The company says the setup pairs its models with Google Cloud's built-in access controls and centralized data governance, which it describes as important for organizations in regulated industries.

OpenAI also says its models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent. OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the partnership an important step in making OpenAI's most capable models and Codex available where customers already build, and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said Google Cloud is focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including OpenAI's.
According to the announcement, general availability is planned in the coming weeks. OpenAI notes that Microsoft remains its primary cloud partner.

stories.title: OpenAI says thousands of AI agents analyzed a brain-cell gene atlas in 32 minutes and turned up new disease leads
paragraphs: OpenAI said on Oct. 21, 2026, that it worked with PerturbAI and Scripps Research to run thousands of AI agents, powered by its GPT-Rosalind model, over existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells. According to OpenAI, the analysis took 32 minutes, and the team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, done one gene disruption at a time, would take months to a year.

The data came from a whole-brain CRISPR atlas, which shows how disrupting individual genes affects different types of cells across the mouse brain. OpenAI says each agent investigated one gene disruption, analyzed the cells' responses, searched the scientific literature and proposed explanations, and the reports were combined into a 'reasoning atlas' linking genes, cellular effects, publications and possible mechanisms. OpenAI says the agents reproduced findings from human analyses, and that their judgments of novelty and scientific value matched those of blinded human experts.

Among the leads OpenAI describes: in the cerebellum, disrupting the gene Tsc2 changed the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication while disrupting its partner Tsc1 changed little, a difference OpenAI notes may be relevant to tuberous sclerosis. The agents also linked disruption of Dctn1, a gene whose mutations cause the Parkinson-like Perry syndrome, to higher activity of cholesterol-making genes, raising a question about cholesterol and neurodegeneration that human experts called novel and worth following up.

OpenAI also compared the approach with a single agent given the whole dataset using the same model and resources. At the largest workload, it says, the distributed agents cited more than 700 references versus 11 for the single agent, and blinded human experts preferred the distributed-agent reports 75% of the time. OpenAI says the reasoning atlas is available for researchers to explore and that the findings still need lab experiments to test the proposed mechanisms.

stories.title: Anthropic says Claude designed 17 lab-confirmed protein binders against dangerous scorpion toxins
paragraphs: Anthropic said on Oct. 20 that it asked an internal research model, working inside Claude Science, to design minibinders, small proteins that attach tightly to a target, against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that such binders could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. The company says the project grew out of a question from the investment research firm Citrini Research about whether AI could let motivated nonexperts tackle a real health problem. Anthropic notes that scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more each year, causing more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in places with limited medical care.

According to Anthropic, the model worked mainly autonomously for 64 hours from an initial prompt plus four follow-ups. It used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 protein designs, screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs and picked 180 designs for testing, and the team added 31 more with Claude's help. The targets were five neurotoxins from scorpions in Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II) and the Middle East (LqhIII). Anthropic says the campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.

The contract labs Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience tested all 211 designs, and 17 met Anthropic's strict criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin: seven against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I and two against LqhIII. None of the designs aimed at several toxins at once worked against more than one, and Anthropic's X thread says none bound the Brazilian species' toxin. The two strongest, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, bound Cn2 with affinities in the single-digit nanomolar range, and competition tests suggest they attach at or near the same site as an antibody reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice.

Anthropic stresses that this is exploratory work and that it is not claiming to have produced an antivenom: the binders were tested only against lab-made toxins, not for neutralization in cells or protection in animals. Two outside experts it consulted, Susana Vázquez Torres of Spain's National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO) and Timothy P. Jenkins of the Technical University of Denmark, called it a promising first step. Anthropic is releasing all 211 designs and their lab data on Hugging Face.

stories.title: Mathematicians say an OpenAI proof of the 'quasi-Riemann hypothesis' looks correct, calling its implications 'staggering'
paragraphs: Number theorists who have spent the past two weeks studying an AI-generated proof released by OpenAI on Oct. 6 largely agree that it is correct, Quanta Magazine reported on Oct. 19. The proof claims to settle the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, which has been open for more than 160 years and concerns how prime numbers are distributed. Jared Duker Lichtman of Stanford University called it "the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin," and Maksym Radziwiłł of New York University told Quanta the implications are "staggering," adding that "the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH."

Quanta explains that the Riemann hypothesis says all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have a real part of 1/2, while the quasi version only asks for proof that they lie in a vertical strip narrower than the known one between 0 and 1. According to Quanta, OpenAI announced two versions: one dated Sept. 30, 199 pages long and formally verified in the Lean programming language, placing the zeros between 1/8 and 7/8, and a 49-page version completed almost a week later, not yet formally verified, placing them between 1/12 and 11/12. Mathematicians have focused on the shorter paper, which Quanta says is the only one of OpenAI's Oct. 6 papers to have been edited by a person; OpenAI told the magazine, "The paper is the result of work from everyone at OpenAI."

Radziwiłł told Quanta that both papers are "horribly written," falling well short of the field's standards of clarity, but that he can now sketch the argument in half a page. Experts quoted by the magazine say the proof introduces no new concepts and instead combines long-known ideas, including obscure objects called metaplectic forms and a formula that Radziwiłł and Alexander Dunn of the Georgia Institute of Technology proved in 2021. Quanta reports that Princeton's Peter Sarnak has repurposed a course he is teaching this semester to study the proof, and that he said he won't be satisfied it is "a Theorem" until humans check and understand all the details.

According to Quanta, mathematicians expect the result to establish many other results in number theory, geometry and theoretical computer science, but they are skeptical that the same techniques can reach the full Riemann hypothesis. "It seems most likely to me that once mathematicians have fully internalized the new methods and worked through their implications, we will still feel as far off from the full Riemann hypothesis as we were before," Will Sawin of Princeton told the magazine, adding, "But I am not certain of this."

stories.title: SpaceX will try to catch both stages of Starship on its next test flight, targeted for November
paragraphs: SpaceX will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 20, Space.com reports. According to Space.com, Musk said that if it succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," and he called it "a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness." Musk did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.

Space.com describes Starship as the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked, with both stages, the Super Heavy booster and the Ship spacecraft, designed to be fully and rapidly reusable. Unlike the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters, which land on pads or on ships at sea, Super Heavy and Ship are meant to steer themselves back to their launch tower, which captures each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms. Space.com notes Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030.

Starship has flown 14 test flights so far, and SpaceX has caught Super Heavy with the chopsticks on three of them, Space.com reports, but the company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which travels higher, farther and faster than the booster. Musk said he thinks it is "more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," and that if not, SpaceX has "a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year." On Flight 14, on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites, according to Space.com.

The Flight 15 preview was an aside on a call mainly about SpaceX's finances, Space.com says. Company representatives reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from $5.6 billion in the same quarter of 2025, and net income of $4.4 billion, compared with a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier. Space.com reports that only $1.8 billion of the quarter's revenue came from the launch division, with most of the rest coming from Starlink connectivity and artificial intelligence.

stories.title: NASA's Perseverance rover sets the record for the farthest drive on another world: 28.10 miles
paragraphs: NASA's Perseverance rover has set a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body, according to a NASA Mars 2020 mission blog post published Oct. 21 and a NASA release carried by ScienceDaily. On Sol 2006, which was Oct. 11, 2026, its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), writes Vandi Verma, chief engineer for robotic operations at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. ScienceDaily reports that this beats the previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) held by NASA's Opportunity rover, which explored Mars from 2004 to 2018, and that Opportunity needed nearly 15 years to cover that distance while Perseverance did it in about five and a half years. Verma writes that the rover's engineering twin on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records.

Verma explains that two months earlier, on Sol 1947, the odometer sat about 200 meters short of the milestone, but the rover spent time in a scientifically interesting area doing short drives for rock abrasions and close-up science on ancient outcrops before it moved on and sailed past the record. ScienceDaily reports the record came as Perseverance headed toward a location called "Idubi," in an area beyond the western rim of Jezero Crater known as "Lac de Charmes," which may contain some of the oldest terrain ever examined in the solar system. At Idubi, according to the release, scientists hope to find evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, where heated water once circulated through rocks.

Both sources credit the rover's autonomy. ScienceDaily says the AutoNav system builds a three-dimensional map of obstacles as the rover moves and picks a safe route, letting it cover as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single Martian day, and that AutoNav has evaluated the terrain for more than 90% of Perseverance's driving, compared with about 5% for the early autonomy on Spirit and Opportunity. Verma writes that the team raised the rover's tilt limit to 24 degrees, updated its braking and steering software, and added a capability called onboard Global Localization, which uses the processor in the Ingenuity helicopter base station to compare ground and orbital images and locate the rover "as though we had GPS on a world without it."

"The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We've blown well past that," JPL project manager Steven Lee said, according to ScienceDaily. The release says NASA has approved Perseverance's first mission extension, which began in October and runs through about the end of 2028, and that the rover has gathered 29 samples of rock and regolith so far. It adds that Perseverance has also passed the distances driven on the Moon by the Apollo 17 astronauts in 1972 (22.2 miles) and the Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973 (24.2 miles).
